entries.summary_and_credibility_md: The CMS OSPO's main toolkit. It packages the five-tier maturity model with a script that works out a project's tier, templates that generate the files each tier needs, a release checklist per tier, Repolinter configs that flag missing files, GitHub Actions that push template updates, and a generator for code.json (the metadata file federal agencies use to inventory their code). It came out of a collaboration between USDS, HHS, the Digital Service at CMS and U.S. Digital Response, and is actively maintained (about 1,200 commits, 48 stars, 19 forks). It's public domain (CC0), but built for federal requirements, so parts would need adapting for City rules. It also depends on Repolinter, which was archived in February 2026.
entries.relevant_content_md:
- Largely automates a lot of the heavy lifting that we would be tasking the OSPO with
- *Gap filled:* code.json gives every repo a standard metadata file. An NYC version could be the basis for the Catalog function.

entries.label: DoW CIO 2026
entries.title: DoW Open Source Software FAQ (GitHub version)
entries.citation_md: Office of the DoW CIO. 2026. *United States Department of War Open Source Software FAQ.* GitHub Pages version, repository risacher/DoD-OSS-FAQ. Last updated July 28, 2026. https://risacher.github.io/DoD-OSS-FAQ/. Accessed November 11, 2026.
entries.summary_and_credibility_md: The Defense Department's open source FAQ, now styled Department of War, published from a GitHub repository. The byline is the Office of the DoW CIO, and the date matches the version on code.mil (see Code.mil 2026), so this looks like the same FAQ in its working form. The repository's README calls it an "experiment in collaborative tools for public engagement" on policy documents, and anyone can suggest changes by pull request. It's an official source and calls itself an educational resource, not legal advice. Its answers rest on federal and DoD law, so they don't apply to the City directly. The repository is small (16 stars, 5 forks, 8 commits), and its license isn't stated on the page.
entries.relevant_content_md:
- **Model for an NYC FAQ.** A policy FAQ kept on GitHub that anyone can suggest changes to. An NYC open source FAQ could be maintained the same way, next to the Open Data Technical Standards Manual the City already keeps on GitHub. Fits the *Toolkit* and *Guardrails* sections
- **Open source is commercial software.** Under the DoD CIO's 2022 memo, open source "meets the definition of commercial computer software," so it gets equal consideration with proprietary products. Federal market research has to consider it. TODO: is there a City procurement rule that treats it the same way?
- **Sharing is not public release.** The FAQ separates the SHARE IT Act's government-wide sharing from releasing code publicly: sharing is "not the same thing as public release as OSS." Useful for the executive summary: an inventory and sharing between agencies come first, and public release is a separate decision
- **Open by default.** The 2022 memo says software not tied to national security "should be open-by-default and released (under an open source software license)" unless specific conditions apply
- **Staff can contribute.** The 2022 memo authorizes government employees to contribute to open source projects as part of their official duties. A model for the participant stage
- **Security.** "Merely hiding source code does not counter attacks." Security depends on review and timely fixes, and both open and proprietary software need case-by-case evaluation. Good answer to the most common objection
- **Support is required.** Community support alone isn't enough. The 2022 memo requires a support and sustainment plan, and support for open source "is often sold separately." Backs the *Support* function
- **Evaluating open source.** Judge it on need, cost and risk, using total cost of ownership over the system's life. Points to outside frameworks such as QSOS and OSMM. A ready-made input for Haddad's classification scheme
- **Migration.** Summarizes guidelines that start with non-critical systems and avoid ties to proprietary formats. Supports phasing the work in
- **Who owns the code.** Under current DoW contracting, "the contractor usually retains the copyright for software developed with government funding," though the government can release code it holds unlimited rights to. TODO: what rights does the City get in its software contracts?
- Several answers are federal-only (the Antideficiency Act, Navy and Army rules, federal copyright rules) and don't carry over to the City

entries.label: Haddad 2022
entries.title: A Deep Dive into OSPOs
entries.citation_md: Haddad, Ibrahim. 2022. *A Deep Dive into Open Source Program Offices: Structure, Roles, Responsibilities, and Challenges.* Foreword by Chris Aniszczyk. The Linux Foundation. https://doi.org/10.70828/TDWK4785
entries.summary_and_credibility_md: A Linux Foundation Research report on how OSPOs are set up: where they sit in an organization, what they do, how they're staffed and the problems they run into. Haddad leads LF AI & Data Foundation and draws mainly on corporate OSPOs, so public-sector cases are thin. However, it describes the structures most directly applicable to corporate OSPOs, which generally assumes different internal structures and greater budget availability than we can expect for a municipal OSPO.
entries.relevant_content_md:
- Marketing language

*Where NYC stands*

- NYC gov is currently in the ad-hoc stage 0 of the maturity model, meaning agencies are consistently using OSS internally. Moving into stage 1 means committing to compliant licensing, educating developers, and inventory tracking.
- *Gap filled:* Haddad on where OSPOs start: "In general, an organization forms an OSPO when it realizes that its people are consuming open source products and code. This usage is typically internal rather than part of its products or services to its customers or users." (p. 9). This is where NYC is now
- *Gap filled:* "The common starting point is the adoption of OSS and integration of OSS in products and services." "Typically, the early stages are engineering-driven due to engineers using open source components" (p. 16)
- *Gap filled:* Stage 0 in his words: "the earliest form of adoption is ad hoc due to developers solving problems using readily available tools and technologies" (p. 9). He calls Stage 1 "Legal-driven" (p. 8)
- TODO: quotes were pulled through a summarizing tool; check wording and page numbers against the PDF before quoting: https://www.linuxfoundation.org/hubfs/LF%20Research/LFR_LFAID_Deep_Dive_Open_Source_Program_Offices_081922.pdf

*Structure*

- The most applicable OSPO structure example appears to be a Virtual OSPO in which there is a Head of Open Source (for NYC perhaps a small team) who works with a team composed of individuals from different teams who dedicate a certain percentage of their time to support the OSPO. This typically does not have a dedicated budget; dedicated spending would come through OTI.

*Staffing*

- Lists the following roles as needing to be covered by the hired staff:
  - Head of OSPO who has a comprehensive understanding of open source first and foremost, strong technical background, knowledge of licensing and industry best practices, who is connected to the OSPO communities etc. I believe this would likely be the primary hire.
  - Senior engineer, ideally a full-stack generalist like those hired to PIT Crew.
  - Technical evangelists who do the public work and technical documentation that build critical support. Currently we are serving that function.
  - Compliance engineer responsible for licensing obligations
  - Legal counsel, general not in-house.
- I believe the roles of several of these could be combined. The OSPO's head would likely be responsible for evangelist work that needs to be done alongside champion counterparts already within OTI.

*Strategy: the Consumer stage*

- There are four stages of strategy with open source code: consumer, participant, contributor, and leader. For our initial purposes and marketing, NYC's OSPO is a consumer. Strategic consumption would mean:
  - Reviewing all open source activities, including license compliance
  - Build a classification scheme to determine which OSS to consume, with explicit criteria such as availability of features, maturity of source code, size/composition of the dev community etc.
  - Inventory OSS used throughout NYC gov via SBOM to identify unmet license obligations and identify security vulnerabilities.
  - Deploy automated workflow software for evaluating open source usage. This would mean metrics pulled through the GitHub API and git logs, automated security checks, repo scaffolding and CI harnesses that run checks every time code is deployed. This meta layer scales horizontally across repos.
- A plan for incremental investment in headcount and infrastructure is also mentioned, though we may not include that at this time.
- Strategy needs to be communicated throughout OTI with education for staff. Encourage them to identify and adopt, be transparent about tooling, subscribe to mailing lists, attend conferences, join OS foundations, host events and invite other community members to present.

*Looking ahead: the Participant stage*

- Moving into the Participant stage would be an eventual necessity, and beyond would be phenomenal for NYC's visibility in the world of technological governance, but we are not there yet. But it may be strategic marketing to project 'Where We Could Go from Here.' Some of the highlights are:
  - File bug reports, contribute fixes, improve or extend functionality, implement new features, or take security measures to improve NYC's products
  - Contribute source code from internal development to demonstrate good faith and status
  - Many others but these will land the most cleanly from a gov product standpoint

*Compliance and outside organizations*

- Significant information on compliance; unknown if this is relevant to our messaging at this time, other than to say that an OSPO provides the mechanism for maintaining compliance
- The OSPO should engage with organizations such as the TODO Group and the Apache Foundation, or the Software Freedom Law Center and Open Invention Network if the primary concern is legal dynamics. The relationships may provide resources and legitimacy to the OSPO, especially if the OSPO is making regular product contributions.

*Metrics*

- Metrics should be tracked.
  - TODO: identify who those champions are, and their needs, so we can list the most applicable metrics.
- *Gap filled:* The report itself doesn't list metrics or tie them to champions. It says choosing them is "one of the more difficult tasks for an OSPO" and that "the traditional metrics, which are often used in product organizations, do not apply in the context of open source development. Therefore, new metrics are required" (p. 22). It also notes that many OSPOs "use specialized tools to track their organization's contributions to open source projects" (p. 22). TODO: quotes pulled through a summarizing tool; check against the PDF

*Internal collaboration and education*

- Foster internal collaboration through innersource practices
- The doc identifies education and training of staff as a core function of an OSPO, and this is the key to a successful long-standing bit of infrastructure. We may decide that this is not in scope for this OSPO in its early stages, but I do believe it would be critical to its long-term success and reputation.

*Infrastructure*

- Open Source IT Infrastructure is listed as being critical to function, and it may be a large blocker if OTI's IT infrastructure is too strict for open knowledge sharing and open source contributions.
  - TODO: research IT infrastructure or get someone in OTI to tell us about it.
- Flexibility to communicate with external participants and more blanket approval to contribute to projects will reduce friction

entries.summary_and_credibility_md: A Federal News Network Cloud Exchange interview with Andrea Fletcher, then CMS's Chief Digital Strategy Officer, and Remy DeCausemaker, about six months after the OSPO launched, with a written article by Jason Miller. Federal News Network is a reliable federal IT outlet. The notes below are from watching the full video, so they're the speakers' own points rather than the article's paraphrase. entries.relevant_content_md:
*The case for an OSPO*

- CMS already had many open source projects. The OSPO was a way to make use of that work and do more of it (Fletcher). NYC is in the same position: agencies already use and build open source
- Open source and open source policy weren't new at CMS. What was missing was someone to recognize the ecosystem the agency depends on, make it more secure, and build in the open (Fletcher). Fits the "policy has been sitting there" framing in Myatt 2023
- Building the same thing twice wastes "valuable resources that we don't have enough of." It happens because of separate funding streams and contracts (Fletcher). The same cause likely applies across NYC agencies, so this is good language for the problem section
- The main benefit is innersource: code reused across the agency and the rest of government (Fletcher). Supports "share inside first"
- On contractor-built code that CMS owns: "It was bought and paid for by the American people with taxpayer dollars, it belongs to the American people" (Fletcher). A strong framing line that could be adapted for New Yorkers
- Transparency forces accountability: a hospital can notice a bug and fix it for everybody (Fletcher). Backs the "accountability for contractor performance" outcome

*Answering objections*

- The first myth to clear up: that open source means putting data on the internet. The code that runs on data is separate from the data. Once that was understood, they were "off to the races" (Fletcher). Belongs in Guardrails
- The DoD FAQ helped dispel myths and show that open source is "normal and boring" (DeCausemaker). Supports writing a City FAQ (see DoW CIO 2026)
- Breaking down silos between contractors inside CMS is one of the hard parts (Fletcher)

*Security*

- After Log4J, CMS had to write to each contractor and take their word that the vulnerability wasn't in their software. Automated tools show where the code is and what dependencies and vulnerabilities it has, so fixes go out faster. This was an easy case to make internally (Fletcher). The clearest argument for the SBOM inventory
- CMS runs the OpenSSF Scorecard, from the Open Source Security Foundation, which scores projects on 12+ security metrics (DeCausemaker)
- Repolinter by the TODO Group checks repositories for common problems and runs in automation (DeCausemaker)

*Tools, metrics and results*

- The five-tier maturity model and templates give engineers practical, day-to-day guidance below the level of legislation and regulation (DeCausemaker)
- The tools are used across CMS centers and by the Department of Education (DeCausemaker). Public evidence of reuse outside CMS
- The public metrics site sets a baseline for each project: commits, pull requests and issues, contributors, time to respond to issues, and time to merge a patch (DeCausemaker). A ready list for Measuring results
- Goal: raise the floor for every open source project at CMS, and raise the ceiling for the projects already doing well (DeCausemaker). Good language for the Manage and Support functions
- The office covers inbound code CMS depends on and outbound code it shares (DeCausemaker)
- Modeled on the European Commission, the TODO Group, WHO and CHAOSS (DeCausemaker). Shows CMS drew on the same international examples we cite

*A practical example*

- Hospital price transparency: the law said hospitals' files had to be machine-readable, but not how. CMS built a static open source website where hospitals can check their files against it, a working reference the legislation didn't provide (DeCausemaker). Model for an OSPO turning a legal requirement into a usable tool
  - TODO: is there an NYC requirement (e.g. under the Open Data Law) where a tool like this would help agencies comply?

*People and talent*

- Software is made of code and people. The office helps people meet, breaks down silos, spreads information, makes leaders visible, and gives people a place to come together when new vulnerabilities hit (DeCausemaker). The community building role
- Bringing in early-career talent has been a major impact. Maintenance ("janitorial") work suits students, and they can show it because it's open. It's a recruiting tool for fellows, graduates, and organizations that might contract with CMS (Fletcher)
- Coding it Forward fellows took CMS from 0 to 7 public repositories in 8 months (DeCausemaker)
  - TODO: my notes also say "averaging 2 projects per month," which doesn't match 7 in 8 months. Rewatch to check
- Fletcher calls the whole effort a culture shift

*From the written article*

- *Gap filled:* Fletcher's line on the goal, as quoted in the article: "build it once and be able to reuse it"

entries.label: NYC Open Data Law 2012
entries.title: Local Law 11 of 2012 and amendments
entries.citation_md: New York City Council. 2012. Local Law 11 of 2012 (Int. No. 29-A), "A Local Law to amend the administrative code of the city of New York, in relation to publishing open data." Codified at N.Y.C. Admin. Code § 23-501 et seq. https://intro.nyc/local-laws/2012-11
entries.summary_and_credibility_md: New York City's Open Data Law, sponsored by Gale Brewer and passed by the Council on February 29, 2012. Mayor Bloomberg signed it on March 7, 2012. It required every agency's public data to be on one portal by the end of 2018. The Council added nine amendments between 2015 and 2017, and Local Law 251 of 2017 made the mandate permanent. It's the law itself, so it's the most authoritative source. OTI's Open Data team carries it out, and its "Laws and Reports" page lists every amendment and annual report: https://opendata.cityofnewyork.us/open-data-law/
entries.relevant_content_md:
*What it requires*

- Public data sets go on a single portal, in machine-readable formats, with no registration or license needed
- A Technical Standards Manual that favors open standards. The City keeps it on GitHub: https://cityofnewyork.github.io/opendatatsm/
- Agency compliance plans, updated every year (now published each September 15), with an annual Open Data for All report. The latest is the 2025 Progress Report and Plan
- Amendments:
  - LL 106/2015: archive old versions of data sets
  - LL 107/2015: plain-language data dictionaries
  - LL 108/2015: geocode addresses
  - LL 109/2015: deadlines for answering public data requests
  - LL 110/2015: keep the portal in sync with agency websites
  - LL 7/2016 and LL 244/2017: review FOIL responses for data sets that should be public
  - LL 8/2016: MODA spot-checks agencies
  - LL 251/2017: makes the mandate permanent and requires every agency to name an Open Data Coordinator

*Why it matters for an OSPO*

- NYC has already written "open by default" into local law once. The Open Data Law is the closest local precedent for an OSPO
- It covers data, not source code. Nothing in it requires the City to inventory or share the code it pays for. That's the gap an OSPO would fill
- Open Data Coordinators in each agency are a ready-made model for OSPO liaisons
- The compliance plan and annual report could work the same way for a City code inventory, like the SHARE IT Act's reporting
- The open data team already works in public on GitHub, so OTI has some open-source practice to build on
- A caution: at the Council's February 27, 2024 oversight hearing, Reinvent Albany testified that OTI's open data team was six people. About half of the 872 data sets flagged for automation still weren't automated, and agencies had dropped 22% of the data sets in their plans since 2018. A law isn't enough without staff to run it: https://reinventalbany.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/2024-Reinvent-Albany-Testimony-to-the-NYC-Council-For-Oversight-Hearing-on-Open-Data-Compliance-February-2024.pdf

entries.label: SHARE IT Act 2024
entries.title: Source code Harmonization And Reuse in Information Technology Act
entries.citation_md: Source code Harmonization And Reuse in Information Technology Act (SHARE IT Act). Pub. L. No. 118-187, 138 Stat. 2638 (2024). https://www.congress.gov/118/plaws/publ187/PLAW-118publ187.pdf
entries.summary_and_credibility_md: The federal law requiring agencies to share the custom code they pay for. It was introduced by Sens. Ted Cruz and Gary Peters, with Rep. Nick Langworthy leading in the House, and signed on December 23, 2024. It's the statute itself, so it's the most authoritative source on what federal agencies now have to do. It only covers federal agencies. It doesn't apply to New York City.
entries.relevant_content_md:
- Agencies have to store custom-developed code, plus its documentation and build files, in a public or private repository that other federal employees can reach (within 210 days of enactment)
- Metadata for new custom code has to be public, so other agencies can find it
- When agencies contract for custom software, they have to get rights that let the whole government use, share and change the code
- Each agency CIO writes an agency-wide policy (within 180 days). OMB's Office of Electronic Government sets reporting standards and publishes an annual report of exemptions
- Exemptions: classified and national security code is out automatically. A CIO can also exempt code for export-control or security laws, or an identifiable privacy risk, and has to report each exemption every year
- GAO reports to Congress on implementation within 2 years
- It applies to code written or revised at least 180 days after enactment, so older code isn't covered
- The CMS OSPO maintains the SHARE IT Act implementation guide and tools: the code.json metadata schema, a form and a GitHub Action that generate code.json, and an index generator for agency-wide inventories. Code.gov is the federal inventory: https://dsacms.github.io/share-it-act-lp
- It's a working model for NYC: a short law that turns code sharing from a policy (the 2016 Federal Source Code Policy, which had no enforcement) into a requirement with deadlines and reporting
- code.json could work as-is for City agencies. Databook or govoss could publish a City code inventory in the same format
- TODO: find out whether the 2025 deadlines were met. I couldn't find a public tracker of agency compliance or the first exemptions report

entries.label: Tridgell 2026
entries.title: Coding Multilateralism: the UN's governance of free and open-source software
entries.citation_md: Tridgell, Jennifer. 2026. "'Coding Multilateralism': Implications of the United Nations' Governance of Free and Open-Source Software for International Organisations in the Digital Age." *Computer Law & Security Review* 63: 106384. Published online September 16, 2026. Open access. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.clsr.2026.106384
entries.summary_and_credibility_md: A peer-reviewed, open-access article by Jennifer Tridgell (University of Cambridge) on how the UN moved from scattered, ad hoc use of open source to a coordinated, system-wide approach from 2023. It's the most complete independent account of the UN's open source work, with survey figures the UN hasn't published separately, and the strongest academic source we have for the UN case. It's desk research from public documents, so it maps what the UN has done but doesn't judge how well each initiative works. Notes below are from reading the paper directly (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2212473X26001252).
entries.relevant_content_md:
*The survey: find out what's in use first*

- In September 2023 the UN surveyed 16 of its organizations before writing any rules. All of them used open source "as part of implementing their mandate," and none had a governance framework for open source projects. Model for the Find function: take stock before setting policy
- 72% used open source "with the goal of reducing costs," but only 7% had "allocated a specific budget for [FOSS] costs." The UN's CIO network: open source "is not inherently free and requires ongoing investment in maintenance, training, and governance." Strong support for a budget line in the Cost section
- 22% of surveyed organizations had an OSPO in 2023. By 2024 nearly 47% were establishing one, and 30% had finished

*How the work is organized*

- Open Source United launched in September 2023 under the UN system's CIO network (the CEB Digital and Technology Network), chaired jointly by OICT and UNICC. Its high-level framework was adopted September 28, 2023
- The work is split across six organizations instead of one central office: the ITU wrote the Common Policy Framework, the IAEA and WHO are drafting a common license, UNFPA is building a catalog of open source and potentially open-sourceable software, UNICC runs the shared code platform (on GitLab), and OICT leads training. A model for spreading the work across agencies, which fits Haddad's virtual OSPO
- The Common Policy Framework is phased: four stages and six activities. Licensing and compliance is mandatory from Stage 1; everything else is optional at first and required by Stage 4. An OSPO is one option in the toolkit, not a requirement. Matches Haddad: compliant licensing is the first step

*Scale and setting*

- The UN system is "over 50 UN system organisations with a presence in nearly 4000 locations worldwide." The same coordination problem NYC has across its agencies
- The eight UN Open Source Principles, including "open by default" and "secure by design," are non-binding and were adopted by the CIO network in February 2025. Over 150 signatories as of May 2026, including the governments of France and South Africa, the German state of Schleswig-Holstein, and the City of Barcelona. Endorsing them could be an early, low-cost step for NYC
- Open Source Week is held at UN Headquarters in New York City
- UNICEF has had a GitHub organization since 2007, now with 320 public repositories and over 350 contributors
- The UNDP–ITU Open Source Ecosystem Enabler, supported by the EU, drew 23 applications from 20 countries for two national OSPO pilots. Shows demand for help setting up OSPOs

*Useful quotes*

- Amandeep Singh Gill, the Secretary-General's Envoy on Technology: "Open-source software is everywhere"
- Omar Mohsine, UN Open Source Coordinator, on security: "continuous scrutiny of the code, leading to rapid identification and patching of security vulnerabilities." Fits Guardrails

*A policy alone isn't enough*

- A 2006 UN report already called for an "enabling environment" and system-wide coordination on open source. The author presumes those recommendations weren't carried out. Same lesson as the Open Data Law: a mandate needs people to carry it out

*The author's argument*

- International organizations aren't only adopting open source to save money. They're building and maintaining their own digital infrastructure to protect their autonomy, security and resilience. Where states call that "digital sovereignty," the UN frames it in terms of its immunities and privileges
- Limits she names: desk research only, using public materials that mention open source; covers September 2023 onward; doesn't assess how well individual initiatives work; many policies are still waiting to be put into practice

entries.label: UCL n.d.
entries.title: UCL's Open Source Programme Office: Business Case
entries.citation_md: UCL. n.d. "UCL's Open Source Programme Office - Business Case." University College London, Open Source Programme Office. Accessed November 13, 2026. https://github-pages.ucl.ac.uk/open-source/ospo/business-case
entries.summary_and_credibility_md: University College London's own proposal for creating an OSPO, published on the university's website. No individual author or date is given; UCL's Advanced Research Computing Centre (ARC) is the main supporter. It's a real internal business case rather than research, so it's best used as a model for structure and argument, not as evidence. It's about 4,000 words, much longer than our summary. Two of its links point to google.com instead of their intended pages.
entries.relevant_content_md:
- **The structure our Executive Summary follows:** executive summary; context; what is an OSPO; why the institution needs one, including the risks of not having one; how it would work (plan by year, resources, financial appraisal, governance, supporters); how we'll know it worked; mission, vision and goals
- **Frames the problem as a hidden dependency:** "We do not know how much we depend on it." Close to our point that no one in City government has an inventory
- **Uses a local number to make the risk concrete:** "36.1% of UCL's open-source projects are unlicensed," from the authors' own study of UCL's projects. A model for the New York number we still need
- **A small, staged staffing ask:** 0.3 FTE now, 1 FTE combined in year 1, an aim of 3 FTE by year 5, with 0.2 to 0.4 FTE contributed by each participating department. Similar to the virtual OSPO structure we propose
- **Asks for little new money:** core work comes from refocusing existing staff, with grants sought for extra activities
- **Benchmarks against peers:** CERN, Johns Hopkins and ETH Zurich OSPOs
- **Governance:** a committee with a delegate from each stakeholder area, with public minutes. Similar to our agency liaisons
